title: Semiconductor Devices
subject: Physics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: Classification of solids based on Energy Band Gap E_g at 0 K?
cards.a:
Conductors (Metals): Conduction Band (CB) and Valence Band (VB) overlap, or CB is partially filled; E_g ≈ 0 eV.
Insulators: Completely filled VB, empty CB, very large forbidden gap: E_g > 3 eV (e.g. Diamond E_g ≈ 5.4 eV).
Semiconductors: Filled VB, empty CB, small forbidden gap: E_g ≈ 1 eV (Silicon E_g = 1.1 eV, Germanium E_g = 0.7 eV at 300 K).
cards.hint: At absolute zero (0 K), an intrinsic semiconductor has zero electrons in CB and acts as a PERFECT INSULATOR.

cards.q: Intrinsic Semiconductor: Charge carrier balance and electrical conductivity formula?
cards.a:
Pure, undoped semiconductor crystal. Thermally generated electron-hole pairs: n_e = n_h = n_i (intrinsic carrier concentration).
Total current: I = I_e + I_h = e A (n_e v_e + n_h v_h).
Electrical conductivity: σ = e (n_e μ_e + n_h μ_h), where μ_e and μ_h are electron and hole mobilities (μ_e > μ_h).
cards.hint: Holes conduct in the valence band; free electrons conduct in the conduction band. Electron mobility is always greater than hole mobility.

cards.q: Extrinsic n-type vs p-type Semiconductors: Dopants and majority carriers?
cards.a:
n-type: Pure Si/Ge doped with PENTAVALENT donor impurities (P, As, Sb). Majority carriers = ELECTRONS (n_e ≫ n_h). Donor energy level lies just below CB.
p-type: Pure Si/Ge doped with TRIVALENT acceptor impurities (B, Al, Ga, In). Majority carriers = HOLES (n_h ≫ n_e). Acceptor energy level lies just above VB.
cards.hint: Both n-type and p-type crystals are electrically NEUTRAL overall (total positive charges = total negative charges)!

cards.q: State the Mass Action Law for semiconductors in thermal equilibrium.
cards.a: n_e · n_h = n_i², where n_e is electron concentration, n_h is hole concentration, and n_i is intrinsic carrier concentration at temperature T.
cards.hint: Doping a semiconductor with donors (n_e ↑) dramatically suppresses hole concentration n_h so that their product remains constant n_i².

cards.q: Formation of Depletion Region and Barrier Potential V_b in a p-n Junction?
cards.a:
Electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, leaving behind uncompensated immobile positive donor ions on n-side and negative acceptor ions on p-side.
This space-charge region devoid of free mobile carriers is the DEPLETION REGION. It sets up an internal electric field creating a Barrier Potential (Silicon V_b ≈ 0.7 V; Germanium V_b ≈ 0.3 V).
cards.hint: Internal electric field points from n-side (positive ions) to p-side (negative ions), opposing further carrier diffusion.

cards.q: Forward Bias vs Reverse Bias of a p-n junction diode?
cards.a:
Forward Bias (p-side to +, n-side to -): Applied field opposes barrier field ⇒ Depletion width DECREASES, barrier height lowers (V_b - V), large forward diffusion current flows (mA range).
Reverse Bias (p-side to -, n-side to +): Applied field aids barrier field ⇒ Depletion width INCREASES, barrier height rises (V_b + V), only tiny reverse saturation current flows (μA for Ge, nA for Si).
cards.hint: Under forward bias, diode acts as a low resistance; under reverse bias, as an extremely high resistance.

cards.q: Dynamic (AC) Resistance vs Static (DC) Resistance of a diode?
cards.a:
Dynamic Resistance: r_d = ΔV / ΔI (reciprocal of slope of I-V characteristic at operating point).
Static Resistance: R_dc = V / I.
cards.hint: Dynamic resistance is very small in forward bias (~few ohms) and very large in reverse bias (~megaohms).

cards.q: Half-Wave Rectifier: Diode count, efficiency, and ripple frequency?
cards.a:
Number of diodes: 1.
Output DC Voltage: V_dc = V_m / π ≈ 0.318 V_m.
Maximum Efficiency: η_max = 40.6%.
Ripple Factor: r = 1.21.
Ripple Frequency: f_out = f_in (same as AC mains frequency, e.g. 50 Hz).
cards.hint: Conducts only during positive half-cycles of input AC; completely blocks negative half-cycles.

cards.q: Full-Wave Rectifier (Center-Tapped & Bridge): Efficiency and ripple frequency?
cards.a:
Number of diodes: 2 (Center-Tapped) or 4 (Bridge).
Output DC Voltage: V_dc = 2 V_m / π ≈ 0.636 V_m.
Maximum Efficiency: η_max = 81.2% (twice of half-wave!).
Ripple Factor: r = 0.48.
Ripple Frequency: f_out = 2 · f_in (twice the input frequency! e.g. 100 Hz for 50 Hz input).
cards.hint: PIV (Peak Inverse Voltage): For Center-Tapped = 2 V_m; for Bridge Rectifier = V_m.

cards.q: Filter Circuits in Rectifiers: Capacitor (Shunt) vs Inductor (Series) filters?
cards.a:
Capacitor Filter: Connected in PARALLEL with load. Bypasses AC ripple to ground and maintains steady DC voltage across load. Ripple factor r ∝ 1 / (R_L C).
Inductor Filter (Choke): Connected in SERIES with load. Blocks AC ripple due to high reactance X_L = ωL and passes DC smoothly. Ripple factor r ∝ R_L / L.
cards.hint: Capacitor filter works best with high load resistance (light load); inductor filter works best with low load resistance (heavy load).

cards.q: Zener Diode: Special construction and breakdown mechanism?
cards.a:
Heavily doped p-n junction diode with an ultra-thin depletion layer (~10⁻⁶ m = 1 μm).
Operated in REVERSE BREAKDOWN region.
Zener Breakdown: High electric field (~10⁶ V/m) directly tears valence electrons from covalent bonds (field emission).
Avalanche Breakdown: In lightly doped diodes at higher reverse voltages, thermally generated minority carriers accelerate and knock out secondary carriers by collision ionization.
cards.hint: Zener breakdown occurs below ~6 V with negative temperature coefficient; Avalanche occurs above ~6 V with positive temperature coefficient.

cards.q: Zener Diode as a Voltage Regulator: Working principle?
cards.a:
Connected in REVERSE BIAS in parallel with load resistance R_L, with a series current-limiting resistor R_s.
In breakdown region, voltage across Zener diode remains strictly CONSTANT at Zener voltage V_z, even if input voltage V_in or load current I_L fluctuates.
Current equation: I_in = I_z + I_L ⇒ V_in = I_in R_s + V_z.
cards.hint: Top Board 3-mark derivation! Any fluctuation in input voltage is absorbed as a drop across series resistor R_s.

cards.q: Photodiode: Biasing and working principle?
cards.a:
Operated in REVERSE BIAS. When light photons of energy h ν ≥ E_g strike the depletion layer, electron-hole pairs are created.
Internal junction field sweeps electrons to n-side and holes to p-side, producing an increased REVERSE CURRENT.
Reverse saturation current is directly proportional to incident LIGHT INTENSITY.
cards.hint: Operated in reverse bias because fractional change in minority carrier current is vastly easier to measure than in majority carrier forward current.

cards.q: Light Emitting Diode (LED): Biasing, emission mechanism, and materials?
cards.a:
Operated in FORWARD BIAS. Electrons and holes cross junction and recombine near depletion layer, releasing excess energy as PHOTONS (h ν ≈ E_g).
Materials: Direct bandgap semiconductors (GaAs, GaP, GaAsP), NOT Silicon or Germanium (which have indirect bandgaps where energy is wasted as heat).
Color depends on bandgap E_g (e.g. Red: GaAs_0.6 P_0.4, E_g ≈ 1.9 eV).
cards.hint: Requires a series current-limiting resistor to prevent burnout from excessive forward current.

cards.q: Solar Cell: Biasing and three-step operating process?
cards.a:
Operates with ZERO external bias (no external battery connected; generates electrical power from sunlight).
Three steps: (1) Generation of electron-hole pairs by light photons near junction (h ν > E_g).
(2) Separation of charges by junction electric field (electrons to n-side, holes to p-side).
(3) Collection: Potential difference (photo-voltage) develops across open terminals.
Operates in FOURTH QUADRANT of I-V characteristic graph.
cards.hint: I-V curve lies in 4th quadrant because the solar cell supplies power (acts as a generator), delivering current to external load.

cards.q: Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT): Current relations and current gains α and β?
cards.a:
Current relation: I_E = I_B + I_C (Emitter current = Base current + Collector current).
Common Base current gain: α = I_C / I_E (typically 0.95 to 0.99, α < 1).
Common Emitter current gain: β = I_C / I_B (typically 20 to 500, β ≫ 1).
Relations: β = α / (1 - α) and α = β / (1 + β).
cards.hint: Base is made very thin (~few μm) and lightly doped so that ~95-98% of carriers pass directly to collector (I_B is only 2-5% of I_E).

cards.q: Common Emitter (CE) Transistor Amplifier: Phase reversal between input and output?
cards.a:
There is a 180° (π radians) phase difference between input AC voltage and output AC collector voltage in a CE amplifier!
When input voltage increases, base current I_B increases ⇒ I_C increases ⇒ collector voltage V_CE = V_CC - I_C R_L DECREASES (output swings negative).
cards.hint: Essential Board concept! CE amplifier produces inverted (180° out of phase) amplified output.

cards.q: Voltage Gain A_v and Power Gain A_p of a CE Transistor Amplifier?
cards.a:
Voltage Gain: A_v = ΔV_out / ΔV_in = β · (R_L / R_i), where R_L is load resistance and R_i is input dynamic resistance.
Power Gain: A_p = A_v · β = β² · (R_L / R_i).
Voltage gain in dB: A_v(dB) = 20 log₁₀(A_v).
cards.hint: Power gain equals current gain squared times resistance gain.

cards.q: Three operating regions of a Transistor on Output Characteristics?
cards.a:
1. Cut-off Region: Both junctions (E-B and C-B) reverse biased; I_C ≈ 0 (transistor is OFF / open switch).
2. Active Region: E-B junction forward biased, C-B junction reverse biased (used as LINEAR AMPLIFIER).
3. Saturation Region: Both junctions forward biased; V_CE ≈ 0, I_C is maximum (transistor is fully ON / closed switch).
cards.hint: For switching applications: transistor switches between Cut-off (OFF) and Saturation (ON).

cards.q: Logic Gates: Truth table equations for standard 2-input gates?
cards.a:
AND Gate: Y = A · B (1 only if both A = 1 and B = 1)
OR Gate: Y = A + B (1 if either A = 1 or B = 1)
NOT Gate: Y = Ā (inverts input: 1 → 0, 0 → 1)
NAND Gate: Y = (A · B)̄
NOR Gate: Y = (A + B)̄
XOR Gate: Y = A ⊕ B = Ā B + A B̄ (1 if inputs are different).
cards.hint: NAND and NOR are UNIVERSAL GATES because any Boolean logic function can be realized using them alone.

cards.q: State De Morgan's Laws of Boolean Algebra.
cards.a:
First Law: (A + B)̄ = Ā · B̄ (NOR is equivalent to bubbled AND).
Second Law: (A · B)̄ = Ā + B̄ (NAND is equivalent to bubbled OR).
cards.hint: Break the line, change the sign! (+ becomes · and · becomes +).

cards.q: How to make NOT, AND, and OR gates using only 2-input NAND gates?
cards.a:
NOT gate: Tie both inputs of NAND together (1 NAND gate: Y = (A · A)̄ = Ā).
AND gate: NAND gate followed by a NAND inverter (2 NAND gates: Y = ((A · B)̄)̄ = A · B).
OR gate: Invert inputs A and B using NAND, then feed into NAND (3 NAND gates: Y = (Ā · B̄)̄ = A + B by De Morgan).
cards.hint: Minimum NAND gates required: NOT = 1, AND = 2, OR = 3, NOR = 4, XOR = 4.

cards.q: How to make NOT, OR, and AND gates using only 2-input NOR gates?
cards.a:
NOT gate: Tie both inputs of NOR together (1 NOR gate: Y = (A + A)̄ = Ā).
OR gate: NOR gate followed by a NOR inverter (2 NOR gates: Y = ((A + B)̄)̄ = A + B).
AND gate: Invert inputs A and B using NOR, then feed into NOR (3 NOR gates: Y = (Ā + B̄)̄ = A · B by De Morgan).
cards.hint: Minimum NOR gates required: NOT = 1, OR = 2, AND = 3, NAND = 4, XNOR = 4.

cards.q: If current gain β = 49 in a transistor, find α and collector current for I_E = 5 mA.
cards.hint: Standard MHT-CET 10-second numerical! Remember α is always slightly less than 1.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: If temperature of an intrinsic semiconductor is increased from 300 K to 350 K, what happens to its resistance?
cards.a:
Its resistance DECREASES significantly!
Because semiconductors have a NEGATIVE temperature coefficient of resistance (α < 0). Heating creates more thermal electron-hole pairs, increasing carrier concentration n_i exponentially.
cards.hint: Metals increase in resistance when heated; semiconductors decrease in resistance!
